analysis.one_liner: Extends TV and radio political ad disclosure rules to online ads and blocks foreign-paid political ads on major platforms.
analysis.headline: The Honest Ads Act was introduced with bipartisan sponsorship in May 2019 and sat in the Senate Rules Committee until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021, never receiving a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, TV and radio political ads must say who paid for them, but internet ads do not have to meet the same standard. This bill would apply those disclosure rules to paid online political ads, require large platforms like social networks and search engines to keep a public, searchable file of who bought political ads and how much they paid, and require broadcasters and platforms to take reasonable steps to keep foreign nationals from buying political ads. It responds to the finding that Russian-linked entities bought roughly $100,000 of divisive ads on social media during the 2016 election.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters, who would be able to see who is paying for the political ads they encounter online — including targeted ads that never reach journalists or opponents. It also helps candidates and campaigns on all sides by creating a level playing field: everyone's online ads would carry the same 'paid for by' information that broadcast ads already carry.

how_it_helps.text: The bill extends the 'paid for by' disclaimer rules that apply to broadcast, newspaper, and cable political ads to paid internet and digital communications, with specific rules for how visible the disclaimer must be in text, audio, and video ads [S3].

Large online platforms — public-facing websites, apps, ad networks, and search engines with 50 million or more monthly US visitors — would have to publish a searchable, machine-readable record of political ad purchases, including a copy of each ad, who bought it, the audience targeted, views, dates run, and rates charged [S3].

Each TV or radio station, cable or satellite provider, and major online platform would have to make reasonable efforts to ensure political ads are not purchased directly or indirectly by foreign nationals, closing a gap exposed by Russian ad purchases in 2016 [S3].

The bill's findings note that in 2016 about $1.4 billion was spent on online political advertising, more than quadruple 2012 levels, while disclosure rules still covered only broadcast and print [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Large internet platforms would bear the cost of building and maintaining public ad libraries and policing foreign purchases. Political advertisers, including issue-advocacy groups, would face new paperwork: documenting funders, board members, and purchase details once their yearly political ad spending on a platform tops $500.
analysis.who_pays_short: Major online ad platforms and political advertisers

drawbacks.text: The trigger for disclosure is broad: any ad touching 'a national legislative issue of public importance' counts, which would sweep in issue-advocacy groups and require them to publicly list their executives or board members — a real compliance burden and, critics argue, a friction point for some political speech [S3].

The ban on foreign purchases relies on a 'reasonable efforts' standard rather than a strict liability rule, so platforms would not be automatically liable when a foreign buyer slips through an intermediary [S3].

The bill's own findings say the Federal Election Commission has failed to act on online political ads, and the bill leans on that same agency to write the new formatting and search rules within 90 days — so the quality of enforcement depends on an agency the bill itself describes as inactive [S3].
The record-keeping requirement applies only to platforms with 50 million or more monthly US users, leaving smaller sites and apps outside the disclosure system [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is modest and real: voters would know who pays for the political ads they see online, the same information they already get for TV ads. The costs are compliance burdens on large platforms and paperwork for political advertisers and issue groups, and the foreign-money ban is softer than it sounds because it turns on 'reasonable efforts.' The main design weakness is that enforcement hinges on the FEC, which the bill itself says has failed to act. On balance it is a transparency fix with manageable costs, not a heavy-handed regulation.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill on May 7, 2019 and sent it to the Rules and Administration Committee, which held it; no markup, floor debate, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Amy Klobuchar introduced the Honest Ads Act in the Senate on May 7, 2019, joined by Sen. Lindsey Graham and Sen. Mark Warner as cosponsors, giving it bipartisan sponsorship from the start [S3] [S4].
The bill's stated purpose was to apply the disclosure requirements that govern TV, radio, and print political advertising to internet and digital political advertising [S2] [S3].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Rules and Administration on May 7, 2019 [S5].
The bill's complete action history shows no further action — no committee markup, no floor vote — through the end of the 116th Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large online advertising platforms avoided mandatory public ad libraries and disclosure rules, and the gap that let foreign nationals buy political ads online stayed open. Voters gained nothing because the bill never advanced.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — one Republican and one Democrat joined the lead sponsor — but because the bill never reached a floor vote in a Republican-run Senate, no roll-call record shows where the parties actually stood.

industries.industry: Large online platforms and digital advertising
industries.note: Social networks, search engines, and ad networks would have to build and maintain public, searchable records of political ad purchases over $500 a year and block foreign-funded ads. Their interest in avoiding these rules ran against voters' ability to see who is paying for the ads they see online.

These providers already face political ad disclosure rules, but the bill adds a duty to make reasonable efforts to keep foreign nationals from buying political ads. The added cost is modest and runs alongside voters' interest in knowing who funds election messaging.

Ad buyers would have to document purchaser identity, executives or board members, and targeting details for platform ad records once annual political ad purchases exceed $500. The burden is paperwork, but it applies to all sides equally, so it does not advantage one campaign over another.
